item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Anna Brandenberger, Hanna Mularczyk, and Dora Woodruff (MIT). This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

In late September and early October, we distributed a survey of early career mathematicians. Our goals were to take a “temperature check” of the community, and to give early career mathematicians a centralized, targeted platform to share their views on AI (the survey was not a rigorous data analysis effort). The personal stakes are highest for grad students and postdocs, who face job insecurity and funding instability, so it’s important that our voices are taken into account. We worry that our concerns will be deprioritized, or even misrepresented, without collective resources like this survey.

On October 29th, we posted the results of this survey to the arXiv (history and overview). In the end, over 260 mathematicians filled out the survey, representing around 60 institutions and at least 5 countries. Many of them left free responses in addition to answering the multiple choice questions.

This blog post is an invitation to take a look at the survey results. Some of the results surprised and/or dismayed us: in particular, Question 3.2, Question 3.3, Question 5.2, and Question 6.1, which concern career outlook and research motivation. It’s also important to point out that nearly all of the responses were collected before October 6th, capturing a sample of thoughts from a specific context: we nervously wonder how different this data would look today. As journals, hiring committees, and faculty members make decisions about the future, we urge them to take these survey results into account — and to continue fostering discussions between senior and junior mathematicians.

item.title: What should we teach our (undergraduate) students?
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: [This is a guest post by Jana Gevertz and Steffen Marcus. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] In the last few months AI has hit our discipline with a frightening force. Many of us, understandably, have turned our attention to our students. They are […]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Jana Gevertz and Steffen Marcus. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

In the last few months AI has hit our discipline with a frightening force. Many of us, understandably, have turned our attention to our students. They are absorbing this change while still working out what kind of mathematicians, and what kind of professionals, they hope to become. On this blog, Álvaro Lozano-Robledo recently asked “what should we tell our students?” (What should we tell our students? | What’s new). In this post, we will focus on the natural follow-up question: “what should we teach them?”

Whatever our students choose for their future careers, be it academia or industry, their work will continue to depend on the depth of their mathematical understanding. However, more and more of that work will likely involve prompting, interpreting, checking, and communicating mathematical ideas that an AI model helped generate. Mathematical understanding as we have come to teach it is built on a time-honored tradition of exercise, proof, and computation: struggle with hard problems until a discovery is made, develop a conjecture and make an effort to prove it, compute by hand to uncover a desired result or a pattern that reveals itself. How will our students build mathematical understanding when AI tools can automate the very processes needed to develop it? What does it mean to train new mathematicians?

Presuming society continues to cede more decisions and reasoning to AI, it has been rightly argued that it would be dangerous for these decisions to “rest on reasons that no human community understands” (We’re gonna need a lot more mathematicians | What’s new). In mathematics, as in many other academic communities, understanding begins with undergraduate training that builds off years of education at the primary and secondary level. Without thriving undergraduate mathematics programs, the mathematics community is at risk of depleting the pool of individuals with the capacity to assess work done with (or by) AI and to set the directions of the field.

However, undergraduate education is at an impasse. In our liberal arts style college here in New Jersey, we have struggled with the practical implications of AI on our classrooms while circling more broadly around the question of how our curriculum must change for the future. There is a visceral feeling that our courses need to change, but it’s not clear what that change should look like. The discipline’s conversations so far have centered on our research and publications, our early career colleagues, and our graduate students. The 2026 AMS Committee on Education Workshop Report (2026 AMS Committee on Education Workshop Report | What’s new) highlights the beginning of our efforts to reorganize graduate level curricula with AI in mind. We believe a parallel and continuous effort focused on our undergraduate programs is needed.

This is especially important for our students entering graduate school, as they will be interfacing with mathematics differently than we have in the past. If it is true that “we won’t get to be heroes anymore” (When AI comes for Your Purpose in Life – The New York Times) and we will begin working in larger teams along with AI systems to develop new ideas and proofs, then our training needs to be focused on understanding and robustly checking results presented to us in slightly “alien” forms.

The central problem: teaching understanding

Luckily, this is not really a completely new way of thinking and teaching. After all, undergraduate training has always been about teaching students to check, interpret, and explain results already known to other mathematicians. Whether it be calculations that have been executed time and time again, or proofs of important theorems that are well-established, undergraduate students learn mathematics and shape their understanding using pre-existing knowledge. From that perspective, the basic skills used to interpret, understand, and communicate mathematics learned through an AI system are already a central piece of undergraduate curricula.

However, we cannot simply continue to ignore this technology as a nuisance to our ability to assign homework exercises and hope for the best. We must teach students to work with these systems. And we must find the right way to do so without offloading their ability to think through problems on their own. Our students need both the skillset and the experience necessary to critically validate AI outputs. Whether we like it or not, they will be expected to work in this way with AI systems in their careers. Our coursework needs to carefully train them to develop mathematical intuition, reasoning, and computational skills in concert with this new technology, rather than apart from it, as is our current instinct.

Our pre-AI experience shows that there are distinct differences between productively struggling to re-create existing knowledge and using technology to do this work. Consider an undergraduate student learning strategies of integration in a calculus class. From the student’s perspective, there is something distinctly different about identifying the substitution that transforms a seemingly “impossible” integral into an easily solvable one versus reading through a solution where the substitution has been selected. A student who considered the structure of the integrand to identify an appropriate substitution would indeed have created the result for themselves, despite the expected substitution being well known. A student who instead blindly followed a computer’s (or even their instructor’s) approach without investigating will likely not internalize that changing variables is a foundational mathematical technique that maps difficult problems onto solvable problems.

This is a small example of the difference between teaching the concept versus teaching the computation. This battle has been playing out in our discussions of pedagogy and content since symbolic computation software have become widespread. What has changed is that this conflict has now expanded to the advanced levels of our undergraduate curricula — the newest AI models have come to make our courses a push-button exercise. If our students rely on reading out computer generated proofs and computations exercise by exercise, they immediately lose the critical moments of productive struggle necessary to build mathematical understanding.

Where do we go from here?

As with any debate, there are those who will passionately argue both extremes. Some will say we simply must eschew AI technology by continuing to teach as we always have, relying on in-class pen and paper assessments. This approach fails to prepare our students for a future in which they will need to work efficiently with AI models and manage their output. Others will argue we should throw away our outdated curricula and embrace the transformative power of AI. The risk in this approach is the outsourcing of student learning and understanding, a risk that is simply too high. The answer must lie somewhere subtly in the middle of these two extremes.

In her recent post on this blog (AI, Mathematics, Education, and a public goods problem | What’s New), Gireeja Ranade argues that “we must teach harder, better, and stronger”. Ranade identifies the central issue facing our community as we learn how to teach our students to work with AI models: “we need to train students so that they know what they know and don’t know — students who can identify proof by intimidation and by authority, and have the confidence to push back.” Looking around, it seems the natural inclination for many of us is to revert to how we have taught in the past (perhaps “harder, better, and stronger”) and to ignore the power of AI within the confines of the classroom. Most of us are quietly choosing one of the two extremes.

Indeed, as authors of this post ourselves, we have yet to find the right way to incorporate AI in our mathematical biology or geometry classes this semester, though we have been thinking about it for a while. Adjusting an undergraduate curriculum is difficult and time-consuming work that cannot simply be done on top of the full-time job faculty already do. Reaching a consensus is also going to be very challenging, and even once a curriculum is agreed upon, the work that must follow to redesign course materials is substantial. For these reasons, it is easy to let our undergraduate courses wait three, four, or five more years until we see how everything shakes out. However, our students desperately need us to find this delicate balance more quickly. They need to acquire a breadth of experience interfacing with these systems in their mathematical work now, or they risk getting left behind.

And therein lies the challenge: how do we design undergraduate mathematics curricula that takes such a balanced approach? There have been a number of recent summits, reports, and statements regarding how AI is changing the mathematical landscape and how we should respond. Similar concerted efforts with a focus on undergraduate education are necessary. The MAA Statement on AI in Higher Education outlines some top-down beliefs on how the undergraduate curriculum may have to change. However, much more activity is needed to help guide department leaders and educators on how to make these suggestions concrete. Together we need to work towards a modernized curriculum that considers the following questions.

  • How do we design and implement a curriculum that places a greater emphasis on higher-order competencies, including conceptual and computational reasoning as well as problem solving and modeling (per: MAA Statement on AI)? Efforts to change curricula and teaching in similar ways have often been met with hesitation.
  • How do we incorporate the critical evaluation of AI output into our courses so that students can robustly check these results?
  • Should we be incorporating formalization techniques such as Lean into our upper-level and proof-based courses?
  • Can we reduce the number of topics within each course to create space to focus on reading and interpreting AI output and comparing the answers it gives to the theory students understand to be true?
  • Can we reduce the focus on arduous computations while continuing to emphasize the procedural fluency necessary to critically analyze mathematical arguments?
  • How do engineering, science, social science, business, and health science disciplines see their mathematics, statistics, and data science educational needs changing in the coming years? We certainly must collaborate with related disciplines to thoughtfully consider how moving away from computation to concept and interpretation impacts the training of their students.
  • How do we create courses that emphasize humanized mathematical and statistical communication?

This list is in no way exhaustive, but we do hope it can jumpstart the conversation.

Faculty in all departments need to be thinking hard about how our curriculum should change, before external players force change upon us. Continued leadership from mathematical organizations, including the AMS and MAA, as well as private organizations, is needed. The federal government would also be well-served by offering grants to support the development of innovative mathematics curricula for the AI era. After all, AI technology does not exist without the work of mathematicians. Together, we can work to give our students what they are owed: an education that prepares them to enter a world where they can effectively use AI as a tool, but not as a crutch.

item.title: Futures of Maths Launch
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: [This is a guest post by Francesco Fournier-Facio, Yara Kyrychenko, Jon Roozenbeek, and Julian Wykowski, cross-posted from the Proofs and Prompts blog. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] Today we launch Futures of Maths, a new, living platform that asks active research mathematicians about […]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Francesco Fournier-Facio, Yara Kyrychenko, Jon Roozenbeek, and Julian Wykowski, cross-posted from the Proofs and Prompts blog. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

Today we launch Futures of Maths, a new, living platform that asks active research mathematicians about the most pressing questions around maths and AI. A string of solutions to famous maths problems, found with the help of AI, has provoked a great deal of discussion among research mathematicians. We built Futures of Maths to understand how mathematicians are dealing with this change in their research and teaching, and where they see the field heading.

How it works. The platform shows you short statements about maths and AI. You rate each one from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”, or skip it, and you can mark the ones you find exceptionally important. Once you have answered, you see how everyone has rated the statement so far. You don’t have to finish in one go: you can leave and come back at any time. Most importantly, you can post your own statements. A moderator checks each one, and then everyone else can rate it, so the set of statements keeps evolving with the community’s input.

Results. Once we have collected enough responses, we will publish the results and make them available to the community. We will post again on Proofs and Prompts when this happens.

Who can participate. You can take part if you are 18 or older and have at least one article published in the last 5 years in a mathematics journal, meaning one indexed by zbMATH Open (recently accepted articles also count). The quickest way in is to sign in with ORCID. The article must be on your public ORCID record, added by Crossref. Articles you enter yourself don’t count. If it isn’t there, accept Crossref’s permission request in your ORCID inbox and make the work public. If that doesn’t work, for example because your article is accepted but not yet published, you can request a manual review from your institutional email address. We review these case by case.
We appreciate that this is only an approximation of what an active research mathematician is, but we chose it for its simplicity, objectivity and efficient verifiability. We welcome proposals of alternative criteria that cover a more representative sample, and have these same three qualities, they could be implemented in future iterations.

Privacy. The survey is anonymous. Verification happens on a separate website, and the survey itself never learns your name, email address or ORCID iD. When you first register, you receive a personal link that lets you return as often as you like as the consultation evolves. Please save this link. We can’t look it up or resend it, because that is what keeps you anonymous. Questions about yourself are optional, under “My session”, and you can withdraw your answers at any time.

Inviting wide participation. The results will only be meaningful if a large and diverse group of people takes part, both proposing statements and rating them. Please share this widely, and especially with people whose point of view you feel is underrepresented in the discussion on maths and AI.

If you have any suggestions or feature requests, please leave them in the comments!

My own views on these topics (which often overlap with, but are not identical to, those of the guest authors) are […]
item.content:encoded:
I am continuing in this current era to open up my blog to a broader range of voices on math and AI, with the majority of posts now being guest posts by other authors. My own views on these topics (which often overlap with, but are not identical to, those of the guest authors) are summarized on this page. I have also given a number of recent interviews and talks on these topics; I am listing some of these here for reference.

  • “How maths underpins almost every aspect of our lives“, Instant Genius podcast, BBC Science Focus, October 18, 2026.
  • “Terence Tao & Yu Deng: Why We Build Open Math Model“, SAIR Foundation, October 19, 2026.
  • James Tapper, “Terence Tao: AI race turns beautiful mathematics into ‘toxic waste’“, The Observer, October 23, 2026.
  • “Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world“, World View op-ed, Nature, October 22, 2026.
  • “Terence Tao on how AI math solutions miss the point“, interview with Flora Lichtman, Science Friday, October 28, 2026. [Youtube version]
  • “Inside AI’s Brutal Race to Solve a Famous Math Problem“, New Scientist, October 28, 2026.
  • Rivka Galchen, “The Year Math Changed Forever“, The New Yorker, November 1, 2026.

Disclosure: while many of these articles were solicited due to current events, some are also related to a long-planned launch of a book I wrote, to be released Nov 10.

item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by the AHM communications group. — T.]

We are happy to announce that the Teaching Working Group of the Association for Human Mathematics wrote a set of recommendations on doctoral advising aimed at departments, advisors, and students. The document contains five guidelines centered on prioritizing human-authored writing, avoiding overreliance on AI, confronting the ethical concerns of AI use, and improving the wellbeing of students, as well as concrete proposals on how to implement them. We encourage everyone to read and share the document, and we especially look forward to feedback and suggestions.

item.title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: [This is a guest post by Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai, and Jie Xue. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] This is a good time for mathematicians to think carefully about the purpose of their work. The development of artificial intelligence brings that question […]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai, and Jie Xue. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

This is a good time for mathematicians to think carefully about the purpose of their work. The development of artificial intelligence brings that question before us with unusual force. Much of the discussion concerns which tasks machines will perform and which abilities will remain distinctively human. But our response also depends on a prior question: what do we understand mathematical work to be, and what gives it its worth? If our answer has become inseparable from the production of results and the demonstration of individual ability, the present uncertainty may reveal a difficulty in our conception of the work itself.

There are broadly two perspectives on mathematics. According to one, we invent it as we construct it: we introduce concepts, choose axioms, and develop theories. According to the other, mathematics exists independently of these activities, and our task is to discover it. These perspectives need not disagree about every aspect of mathematical practice. We plainly develop formalism and arguments. The deeper question is whether the truths we come to understand owe their existence to these acts, or whether our constructions enable us to recognize something that does not depend on us.

While discovery of mathematical truth can sound passive, a paleontologist searching for fossils must decide where to excavate, develop techniques, and recognize the significance of incomplete remains. The fossils existed long before the investigation, but finding them may require extraordinary imagination. Their prior existence gives direction to the investigator’s activity. Similarly, a mathematical discovery may require the invention of an entire language and framework through which a previously unnoticed relationship becomes intelligible. The discovery may require great creativity, but that does not make the truth discovered a creation of the individual. We encounter this distinction whenever our constructions surprise us. A definition introduced for one purpose reveals an unexpected connection elsewhere. A conjecture that seemed to organize our examples admits a counterexample. Two theories developed through different questions turn out to express a common structure. In each case, our thought encounters something it did not freely determine. We can revise our definitions or abandon our conjecture, but we cannot make the original argument valid merely by wishing it so.

The Platonic perspective gives a natural account of this independence. On this view, there were infinitely many primes before anyone proved that fact. Mathematical truth neither waits for our recognition nor receives its authority from it. We may choose how to describe a structure, but we do not choose its properties in the same way. This perspective also changes the place of the mathematician. Our intelligence becomes a means through which an order independent of us can be understood. The significance of the work lies in its relation to that order.

The distinction between a correct derivation and an understanding of its significance is equally important. An axiomatic system permits indefinitely many deductions, but the ability to produce them does not by itself supply a worthy direction of inquiry. Mathematical statements may be formally correct without being enlightening. We can introduce countless definitions and prove countless statements about them. What makes one definition illuminating? Why does one theorem disclose something fundamental while another merely adds to the available material? These questions concern the relation of a particular investigation to the principles it brings into view. Mathematical taste has a place here, provided we understand it as more than individual preference. We value a theory when it reveals a unity among things previously understood separately, or enables us to recognize why a phenomenon occurs. Although mathematical truths may exist independently of us, their discovery can transform our understanding and enrich our experience of the world. The ability to carry out longer chains of reasoning does not by itself explain such understanding. Reasoning serves understanding by articulating relationships and making their justification explicit. However, the success of reasoning does not mean that all knowledge can be reduced to it. Nor does our ability to reason more extensively determine what is worth knowing or why we seek knowledge.

Mathematics is only one field of knowledge. Not everything can be understood mathematically, nor is mathematical achievement the ultimate purpose of intellectual life. Yet we increasingly measure intellectual life through publications, citations, awards, and other indicators of performance. While useful, these measures become problematic when they define the worth of the work itself. We begin to see mathematicians as collections of productive abilities, and mathematics as merely their output. From this perspective, anxiety about being replaced by AI is natural: a machine that performs these tasks better appears to threaten our worth. But the problem began before AI arrived. We had already come to understand ourselves in terms suited to machines. AI merely exposes the consequences of this view.

The response cannot simply be to seek refuge in distinctively human abilities such as creativity, intuition, or taste. If we value these abilities primarily because they give us an advantage over machines, we remain trapped in the same conception of intellectual worth. Why should the value of our pursuit depend on being better at it than someone or something else?

Mathematics offers an opportunity to reconsider this whole orientation. Its truths do not become more true through the distinction of the person who expresses them. In understanding a proof, we bring our thought into conformity with a relationship whose validity does not belong to us. The particular path by which we arrive may bear the marks of our individuality. What is understood is available beyond that individuality. We can allow this experience to loosen the belief that knowledge has its highest value as an achievement attributable to ourselves.

Egoless mathematics begins with taking that possibility seriously. Humility then reaches beyond modesty about our accomplishments or generosity in sharing credit. It concerns the place from which we pursue knowledge. We may seek truth to serve our existing purposes, or allow what we discover to change those purposes themselves. If we approach truth on the condition that its discovery must preserve our importance, we have already made it subordinate to ourselves. Accomplishing this reordering can be demanding, as intellectual sophistication can furnish elaborate defenses of the very attachments that prevent us from understanding. What matters is whether our abilities remain answerable to truth, including when it requires us to reconsider what we have been using those abilities for.

From this perspective, the possibility of mathematical discoveries through AI need not be a source of sadness about our purpose. A truth has become accessible; its worth is not diminished by the absence of our authorship. We need not immediately turn the event into a judgment about our relative importance. The search can continue without requiring every advance to vindicate the seeker. Indeed, the demand for such vindication has always burdened the pursuit, whether the competing claim came from another mathematician or from a machine.

The opportunity before us is therefore more substantial than a rearrangement of mathematical labor. It invites us to reconsider what gives an intellectual life its worth, and to let the pursuit of truth shape not only our work but also how we approach life.

This may sound like asking us all to become saints. Insofar as it asks us to grow in virtue and relinquish our attachment to our own importance, that impression is not far from the truth. But virtue is not something to cultivate for the admiration of others. It is necessary for genuine joy, even in our work. The satisfaction of solving a difficult problem or winning a prize can be fleeting when it rests on our standing relative to others. The joy of understanding is different. Something previously obscure becomes clear, and we recognize a beauty that does not diminish when someone else discovers it first. We can share this joy without depriving anyone of it. Growing in virtue allows us to experience it more fully, free from the need to establish our own importance.

This perspective may also help reconcile two positions within the mathematical community regarding AI. Some are comfortable with or even enthusiastic about using AI, but wish to develop appropriate processes and principles for its use. Others prefer not to use AI at all. Both positions have their merits. Egoless mathematics offers a way of reconciling them by introducing a higher consideration: both approaches can reflect the same underlying commitment to mathematical truth, regardless of how we choose to pursue it. Our aim here is not to settle particular questions of policy, but to develop a higher-level perspective that can guide our deliberations and ultimately our actions.

Seen in this light, we need not be afraid of what AI may achieve in mathematics. Mathematics was beautiful before any of us were born, and it will remain beautiful long after we are gone. Its worth does not depend on our accomplishments, nor does our joy in understanding it have to depend on being the ones who make the discoveries. Our purpose rests on our willingness to let truth govern what we seek and what we become.

We, the authors of this essay, are still far from having attained such egolessness. Nevertheless, we recognize it as an ideal toward which we wish to strive.

We conclude with a thought experiment. Ramanujan is reported to have said, “An equation has no meaning for me unless it expresses a thought of God” (Robert Kanigel, The Man Who Knew Infinity, 1992). If he were alive today, witnessing the advances of AI in mathematics, would he be perturbed by what they might mean for his purpose as a mathematician?

Statement of AI Usage: While the ideas expressed here are entirely our own, we gratefully acknowledge the assistance of GPT Astra 6.0 and GPT 6.1 Sol in drafting this post.

item.title: Mathematics has changed. Let’s act like it
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: [This is a guest post by Frank Calegari. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] Why we should not be sad The release by OpenAI on October 6 of over 700 research papers was a watershed in the history of mathematics. AI is now undeniably […]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Frank Calegari. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

Why we should not be sad

The release by OpenAI on October 6 of over 700 research papers was a watershed in the history of mathematics. AI is now undeniably capable of making groundbreaking contributions across many areas of mathematics. So why are some mathematicians so unhappy?

Some of it is the apparent disregard by AI companies for the practice of mathematics. The OpenAI papers — despite some tremendous ideas — are atrociously written and violate our community expectations of attribution. Some of them are even wrong. We have much more control over how we hire mathematicians, publish papers, and train students than over the behavior of trillion-dollar companies, and that is where our efforts would be better spent.

Much of the reaction seems to reflect a feeling that the subject that they love is under attack, and is being “hollowed out”. The recent OpenAI dump made barely a dent on the general problems of functoriality and reciprocity in the Langlands program. But even if it had solved every problem in the Langlands program, to imagine that would have “solved number theory” would be as naive as saying that the construction of the periodic table solved chemistry. Mathematicians should do a better job explaining that when we talk about the central problems in any area, we are merely discussing the most natural boundaries of our understanding — and that unlocking them is not the end but the first step to finding new playgrounds to explore. Of course, this takes time. I looked for areas of mathematics which were “harder hit”. It is hard not to be struck by Hugo Duminil-Copin’s lament:

Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career (whether in a talk, a lecture, an article, or even a grant proposal) was left untouched by the announcement. Everything has been claimed to be proved.

I expected to see a few of them in the list. But not all of them. Not all at once. Not with such nonchalance.

How would I respond to that?

The classification of finite simple groups.

I can’t say much about percolation theory, but there is another historical precedent I think mathematicians should take note of. In 1972, Dan Gorenstein announced a program towards the classification of finite simple groups. After a flurry of activity over around a decade, the “classification” was announced by Gorenstein in 1983 (somewhat prematurely, with the case of quasithin groups not being completed for another two decades by Aschbacher and Smith).

The classification of finite simple groups was in many ways a huge success, but it was also a failure in that it — apologies to my group theorist friends and collaborators — cooled a lot of the interest around the subject. The “famous problem” had gone, and mathematicians on the whole turned their attention elsewhere. And yet, there remain very rich questions in finite group theory and even about the classification itself (to name just one: John Conway’s favorite question is why does the Monster group exist?). Perhaps for some fields, the OpenAI dump feels like how a group theorist may have felt in 1970 if the classification was dumped in their office, not in the form of the actual papers, but printed out on a spirit duplicator, smudged a little, then spread randomly like confetti all over the floor.

Right now, we need efforts like that of Gorenstein, Lyons, and Solomon and their work on the revised classification. If this was all we had to do, then it would be a fairly thankless task. But we also have the responsibility not to pronounce the subject “done” but rather — with these new tools available — ripe for further investigation. When mathematicians lament the winding paths missed by the construction of a galactic bypass, they need to realize that those old paths still exist and seek them out. And we need to reward that behavior when it comes to offering people jobs.

The promise of AI, and the (dis)-unity of mathematics:

Since I was 15, I’ve wanted to know what was. First, there was the childhood fantasy of finding a formula that Euler missed. But soon one learns more: how Grothendieck’s period conjecture, together with a sufficiently fine understanding of the geometry of mixed Tate motives (following work of Don Zagier, Sasha Goncharov, Francis Brown, and others) gives a completely satisfying structural, conjectural explanation of what’s going on. The irrationality of , or even its transcendence, is a mere shadow of the actual interesting underlying problem. Apéry’s proof of the irrationality of has inspired me for over years not because of its conclusion, but for how it reveals the tiniest hints of some still secret story relating algebraic -functions to arithmetic.

I hope AI can help mathematicians break out of the straitjacket of being constrained by the first natural conjecture they cannot prove, and work on unraveling the deeper mysteries woven throughout our subject. In the last thirty years, progress in mathematics by humans has been remarkable. But at the same time, I have felt a growing unease; the number of times I have seen mathematicians of all levels being unable to explain to someone even slightly outside their field why what they are doing is interesting has been distressing. The natural grooves of our profession have very much been bent toward more narrow technical expertise than a bigger vision. AI allows us an amazing opportunity to broaden ourselves as mathematicians.

I have tried (not always successfully) to be broad as a mathematician. I had some help by the fact that, while I knew since I was 17 that I wanted to work in algebraic number theory and the Langlands program, I grew up in the crucible of Melbourne University, which was a home to many Thurston students and low-dimensional topologists. This meant I was bathed in the sweet liqueur of hyperbolic 3-manifolds. That exposure has helped my career immeasurably. As with any two deep areas of mathematics, hyperbolic three-manifolds and arithmetic are much more closely connected than would first appear. But it’s still hard to be an expert on both, let alone pursue a crazy idea combining them. Let me get technical for a moment. For every imaginary quadratic field , there are many commensurability classes of compact arithmetic hyperbolic three-manifolds indexed by non-split quaternion algebras . Manifolds in each of these commensurability classes give rise to elements in via the decomposition of into hyperbolic tetrahedra, and their volumes are always rational multiples of . I have always had this idea that one could conceive of elements in these different commensurability classes as forming some type of geometric Kolyvagin system (“Heegner points”) associated to , which one could yoke together by some unknown integral arithmetic version of the Jacquet–Langlands correspondence. This is not a question I have pursued, for two reasons. First, there were so many underlying conjectures involved that any result I could prove was going to be conditional on many of them, something that’s not always appreciated by the mathematical community. Second, assembling all the technical background to formulate such an idea precisely would have taken a huge amount of background work. Now, with AI, the barriers to trying such a problem are much lower. It’s not trying to prove a theorem. It’s trying to explore some completely new direction that may or may not be nonsense. There are so many problems in mathematics that are still so fresh and vital but were previously untouchable that the opportunity to approach them is massively exciting. We need to be more ambitious, to create bold research plans that weren’t even conceivable a year ago.

This is not to say that everyone must (or must not) use AI. But we have to rethink and readjust what’s important. Proofs of major conjectures, using AI or otherwise, are going to remain part of the new mathematics. But working toward broader programs (new and old) and structural understanding is going to play a more fundamental role. Christian Szegedy raised the following point:

Mathematics prided itself on being meritocratic, with deep reverence for the explorers: the people who could climb what nobody else could. That specific kind of heroism will matter less, and other skills will matter more: choosing which terrain is worth exploring, steering fleets of airplanes, and explaining what they find to the rest of the world.

I’m ready to board the plane, because I want to see what’s there. At the same time, I would add that people who previously have been walking around on earth with their eyes closed are not going to recognize anything however high they fly; I still believe that many of the skills that mathematicians have now will not only be transferable but vital to the new world order.

The difference in reaction between the optimists and the pessimists is that, for the pessimists, the game is over. For the optimists, the game has just changed. I acknowledge that there are aspects of our mathematical culture that we treasure that won’t survive, and it is only human to grieve that loss. But there now exists an amazing new tool to study mathematics. To turn away and say that the community of mathematics as it currently exists is more important than mathematics itself would be a terrible mistake.

The ugly truth.

For all that everyone has been saying on this blog and elsewhere about how mathematics is about understanding, it takes one look at the arXiv to see many people in our profession rushing out AI-assisted papers in a somewhat unsightly rush to be the “first” to prove things. As many others have noted, there is quickly becoming a gulf between the ability to produce novel proofs and the ability to either demonstrate understanding or push the subject in new and interesting directions. As people crank out more and more results, the Leiden declaration is being honored more in name than in spirit, and it seems like “business as usual” except with a much more compressed time scale and the constant threat of being scooped hanging over people’s heads.

To me, someone who chooses a worthwhile problem, obtains a proof completely using AI, understands it thoroughly, and uses it to develop interesting further questions or directions has made a substantial mathematical contribution. I would give that person substantial credit even if they supplied no new ingredient in the original proof. Choosing worthwhile problems may end up mattering more than producing proofs.

Our obsession with conjectures tends to greatly undervalue the exploratory work that makes answering (or even asking) these problems possible. We are in danger of making that mistake a hundredfold now by encouraging or rewarding the rush for everyone to press the button to get these new results out as soon as possible. I would encourage all senior mathematicians (with the privilege of tenure) to take up the work of creating future problems and exploring new ideas rather than simply using AI to answer existing questions. If you, as a senior mathematician, are stressed about being scooped by AI, then you are not being ambitious enough.

So what are we actually going to do?

Think pieces are ultimately pointless unless they propose some mechanism for actually affecting how people act. The tools that are going to be the most effective are going to be economic rather than rhetorical. Mathematicians want recognition, mathematicians want jobs, mathematicians want grants. The tools that we currently have to affect this are hiring and accepting papers at journals.

Let me offer some very basic concrete suggestions, followed by a few details.

  1. Evaluate all work as if it is AI-assisted.
  2. Make hiring much more about personal interactions rather than a paper file. Interview postdocs and graduate students in person.
  3. Demand more from journals, and abandon those that do not adapt.
  4. Put a greater emphasis on breadth in graduate education, but do not abandon technical skills.
  5. Give better seminars.
  6. Take more ownership of the results of AI.

Evaluations:

Nelson Cole famously spent three years of Sundays discovering the prime factorization

In , this was a contribution to mathematics. Factoring the same number in by hand would be an equally impressive feat of arithmetic, but its contribution to mathematics (even if it had not previously been known) would be far less, since this can be done on a computer algebra system in far less than a second. It’s obvious that AI is changing the economics of what is “easy” or “hard” — much has already been said about the coming collapse of the theorem economy. In time (perhaps quickly) there will emerge a new sense of what remains a substantial contribution to mathematics, whether it be asking interesting questions, developing new programs, or something completely different. In the future, I see no reason to reward a paper based purely on a result that could be produced by machine, whether it was or not. A new proof can still deserve substantial credit for the ideas it introduces, even when its conclusion is already obtainable by machine. So why not start now? Importantly, I do not think this in any way means that access to AI will be required to make progress in mathematics — as long as we continue to value human understanding. While I feel that this is the most controversial recommendation, I also feel it is the most inevitable. It requires relinquishing an aspect of our reward structure that has been around for a long time, but at the same time a structure that will make no sense in the future. Right now, the use of AI carries a stigma, and the phrasing of many AI disclosures reads more like an attempt to minimize the contribution of the machine. If we evaluate every paper as potentially AI-assisted, then we must insist that its authors explain why the mathematics is interesting, what questions it raises, and how it connects to the broader subject. Don’t we want people to be doing this anyway?

Hiring:

It’s not going to be possible to get people to change unless we change how we evaluate people at the level of hiring. Lazy committees in the past have sometimes pointed toward a JAMS paper, an Annals paper, or some other collection of publications to justify how a candidate is impressive. I am looking for a narrative of where you want mathematics to go, the technical ability to explain why this may be possible, being able to converse about many areas of mathematics, and a demonstrable record of having done all of this in the past. This is not in any way a radical new idea. The hiring process is going to have to be much more about personal interactions than a paper file.

It should become standard practice to interview not only for tenure-track jobs, but also for postdocs and graduate student positions. I’m sure we have all had the experience of admitting a graduate student who was “working on higher homotopy theory” to only find out after they are admitted they can’t compute the homology of the circle. At the same time, I have interviewed candidates at the tenure level whom I was initially ambivalent about, but after a 30 minute conversation in my office I was totally convinced that here was someone who not only had a deep vision of mathematics but who was also able to communicate this to their colleagues. Once we take this approach, we then have the responsibility to train our own graduate students to be better able to communicate mathematics, something that we should take much more seriously. Note there is also a difference between knowing mathematics deeply and explaining it fluently; they are related but different skills. Ideally I want both, but it is the first that I ultimately value more highly.

Journals:

The journal system was in dire need of reform even before AI. Our current incentives already are to produce more and more incremental mathematics which is only flooding the system. The radical overhaul required is not going to happen through consensus agreements with editorial boards. (Do you know how hard it is to get academics to agree on anything?) Being accepted by a journal has long since ceased to be a guarantee of correctness (if it ever was) and has simply acted as an imprimatur of quality. I explained above the philosophy of how I think we should evaluate manuscripts going forward. On that basis, I would say that a significant proportion of papers posted to the arXiv should not be published anywhere. If journals demand much more from a paper in terms of writing, ideas, and exposition, I think that would make life better for everyone — editors, reviewers, and even ultimately authors.

If editorial boards are unable to adjust, then a more radical idea is to (at least temporarily) abandon journals altogether. (I still see a place for journals which emphasize exceptional utility and clarity (consider Essential Number Theory)). I am not advocating that people stop writing papers, but removing the fig leaf of journal publication forces the paper to stand on its own merits. Is the paper telling a compelling story? Is it Lean-verified? We should be producing fewer (and better) papers, not more. Autonomously AI-produced proofs, hopefully Lean-checked, also have their place, and should be recorded as part of our collective body of knowledge. (see hexagonmath.)

Graduate students, first-year courses, and seminars.

One of the thorniest issues we face is how to train graduate students. The typical thesis has always been to assign a problem in the overhang, an exercise that will teach the student the technical skills to solve a variation on some old problem, with the expectation that, as they continue, they can expand the techniques they’ve learned to new cases and then hopefully branch out to wider problems. In an age where such a thesis can be produced by the press of a button, we need to re-evaluate based on what we hope a good student will be doing in the future. Even with AI resources, no one is going to be able to explore the links between compact arithmetic hyperbolic three-manifolds and Kolyvagin systems if they don’t know what either of these terms means. (And even if somehow they could, why would they care?) It has become much more important to give students a broader overview of mathematics as a discipline. What I want a graduate student to achieve at the end of their PhD is a view of mathematics that extends well beyond their discipline, and yet with demonstrable technical skills on at least some class of problems. Often, students graduate with technical skills in a subarea, but their experience with other aspects of their area, let alone other areas of mathematics, consists of technical instruction which they have since forgotten, without any real vision. I advocated above that we need to evaluate work as if AI was involved. But this does not imply that we don’t need to teach students to do deep mathematics without AI just as the existence of computers doesn’t mean we should no longer teach children arithmetic.

This has consequences for what we teach, as well as how students learn to talk about it. A graduate course should leave students with some understanding of what the topic makes possible elsewhere in mathematics. We should expect them to retain a sense of the questions and connections, even when they have forgotten some of the technical details.

If we are to evaluate people more on how they can demonstrate understanding in person, we clearly need to be far more conscious of training our students to explain mathematics to other people, either in person, or in seminars, and to their peers. We need to work on giving our students opportunities to learn this skill. Remember that the most successful cohorts of students are the ones who learn together and who talk mathematics with each other.

We should also not forget that not everyone who completes a PhD in mathematics goes on to academia. We should also ask whether the length and structure of doctoral training serve students who will pursue careers outside academia.

Seminars:

Seminars are traditionally where someone presents the details of their latest result. Because math is difficult, this almost always consists of explaining some minor tweak to a previous method, often without anywhere near enough broader context to make it interesting. Instead, seminars should rarely be focused entirely on new work. They should be framed around the broader interesting questions, explaining the avenues on which we are stuck, on which we can make progress, on which we are hopeful, and then perhaps at the very end explaining some novelty, if there is any. This is how I have always encouraged my students to give talks! As senior faculty we all need to be vocal in our seminars demanding more from our speakers.

Ownership.

Mathematicians as a profession would do well to take more ownership of these results. What has come out of the machine has been built on the intellectual foundations of several millennia of human mathematical endeavor. Once you start to take credit on behalf of humanity (rather than attributing these results to either a Silicon Valley tycoon or a mathematical Twitter buffoon), you’ll immediately start to feel much better.

The world is looking at us.

My dean recently visited New York to meet with donors and other friends of the University of Chicago, and everyone she spoke to, regardless of whether they were a math major or not, wanted to talk to her about mathematics. The world is looking at us. There are many many people who care about mathematics without necessarily having a deep technical background (3Blue1Brown has over six million subscribers!). All of my friends in the humanities truly believe that having mathematicians in society both as custodians of one of humanity’s oldest intellectual activities and explorers of the frontiers of knowledge is important. I understand that some part of the culture we so deeply care about will disappear, and as humans, an emotional response to that is very natural. But this is a time to explain to everyone that there are so many great new opportunities, possibilities, and reasons to be optimistic. We are on the verge of a new era of mathematics, and I am excited to see what happens.

Notes:

For more context on Duminil-Copin’s remarks, see also this numberphile video. His full quote also says “We are a resilient community, and I have no doubt that we will adapt”.

Many of the themes mentioned here have been brought up in other posts. To give three examples:

  • The idea that mathematicians should take more ownership of the results produced by AI was also explored in Nestor Guillen’s post.
  • The idea that AI gives us the opportunity to be far more ambitious is raised in Ben Antieau’s post.
  • The idea that we need to revisit our reward structure to create the right incentives was explored in Bryna Kra’s post.

item.content:encoded:
The Academy for the Mathematical Sciences, which is based in the UK, has released a report “The mathematical sciences in an AI-enabled world“. To quote from the release:

The paper examines how recent advances in artificial intelligence are changing mathematical research and its applications, bringing new opportunities for discovery, verification and the use of mathematics across science, industry and society. It also considers the risks associated with these developments and identifies the support and infrastructure needed to realise the opportunities while addressing the challenges.

A central theme is that, as AI becomes increasingly capable of carrying out technical mathematical work, human expertise will be crucial to direct advances. Identifying promising questions, providing key ideas, assessing the reliability of AI-generated results, developing mathematical understanding and translating discoveries into wider use will remain essential.

The paper identifies priorities for the community, including education and skills, independent verification, access to AI capabilities, research assessment, publication and the infrastructure needed to support mathematical knowledge. It sets out areas for action in the near term and over the coming years.

item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by the organizers of the Summit on Math Research in the Age of AI: Dan Freed (Harvard), Larry Guth (MIT), Bryna Kra (Northwestern), Emily Riehl (Johns Hopkins), and Mohammed Abouzaid (Stanford). This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

Last week we organized an intensive two-day summit Math Research in the Age of AI. It was held at the Harvard Center for Mathematical Sciences and Applications (CMSA). Thirty-two mathematicians from academia, government, and industry came together to help navigate this period of rapid change in mathematics and, most importantly, to offer ideas for building the future. There were five working groups organized around the following themes:

  • Evaluation, production, and dissemination of research
  • Coordinated actions for the AI era
  • Open-source tools
  • Formalization in mathematics
  • Collaboration between academia and AI labs

Our report can be found on the summit website. There you’ll also find a link to provide feedback, and we also encourage open discussion in the comments section of this blog.
